title: Live sprinkler and wet system — valve work, draining and isolating
verdict: I would not sign this and I would not send a crew out on it. It is the strongest statement I have read in this set, and I want that on the record: I checked every citation that matters against legislation.qld.gov.au and could not break one. WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) ss 289(2)(e), 289(3)(d), 291(a)(d)(f)(k)(o), 299(4), 58, 425, 78-79 and Part 4.3 all say what the document says they say — s 299(4) really does require a SWMS to describe all control measures considered where the only fall controls are administrative or PPE, addressing s 79(3). WHS Act ss 37, 38 and 39(3) are quoted accurately, including electric shock in s 37(e). Fire Services Act 1990 (Qld) s 146M is verbatim, right down to "(prev s 104D) ... reloc and renum 2024 No. 22 s 56(2)", and s 146N is right. Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 49 is a genuine two-limb test and s 53 really does run the 24 hours from when the maintenance is carried out. Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) is in force; "near" = within 3m of an exposed energised part is s 193, and ss 196(2)(a) and 197 are as described. AS/NZS 1891.4:2025 and AS 2550.10:2025 are real current editions. The water side of the job — the isolation list, lock and tag on every point, prove-it-dead at the drain, both gauges at zero, the booster tag, the handback and the overnight-impairment step — is the best work in the repository. What refuses it is electricity, and it refuses it twice. The statement tells the crew to put a 240 V wet vac and a task light on a plant room floor and plug them in, then deliberately runs hundreds to thousands of litres of water across that floor; the words RCD, safety switch, residual current and extension lead appear nowhere in the file, and shock from the crew's own gear is not in steps[2].hazards. And electric shock as a thing that happens to a person appears exactly twice — as a hazard at steps[3].hazards[2] and as a reporting duty in the emergency section — while the training list promises CPR currency "for anyone working near the pump controller" and the emergency section never cashes it: no "don't touch them", no "kill the supply first", no CPR, no rule that a shocked worker who is walking and talking still goes to hospital. That is the lighting-circuits fault again, in a document that stands a technician at a live pump controller and then floods the room. Underneath those two, steps[8] returns both pump controllers to AUTO before it walks the isolation list and takes the locks off the tank and bypass — the document's own deadhead hazard, produced by its own control order, and the pump control is mislabelled "engineering" which is exactly what ranks it above the real control. Fix the seven findings below and I would sign it; the bones are right.

blocking.field: emergency (whole section — no ELECTRIC SHOCK paragraph exists)
blocking.problem: The document names electric shock twice and responds to it never. steps[3].hazards[2] is "Live 240 V and above at the pressure switch enclosure, tamper switch, jockey pump and fire pump controller". The emergency section's only mention is under NOTIFIABLE INCIDENTS: "a shock off a pressure switch, is notifiable whether or not anyone was hurt" — a reporting duty, not a response. training[4] requires "Provide first aid, HLTAID011, and CPR currency for anyone working near the pump controller", a promise the emergency section never keeps. The INJURY paragraph covers a falling valve cover and riser water in an eye and says nothing about shock. A grep of the whole file for shock, CPR, defibrillator or electrocution returns only hydraulic shock at steps[4].hazards[5], the notification line, and that one training entry. So a crew reading this believes shock is handled: a mate goes down at the controller and the first instinct — grab him — makes a second casualty, and a technician who takes a belt and feels fine goes back to work and arrests in the van.
blocking.fix: Insert a new paragraph in emergency, immediately before INJURY: "ELECTRIC SHOCK. Do not touch the person while they may still be in contact — you will be the second casualty. Kill the supply first: the plug or the board isolator, whichever is faster. If you cannot, push or drag them clear with something dry and non-conductive — a broom handle, a dry rope — never with your hands, never with anything wet. Then ring 000, start CPR if they are not breathing normally, and send the second person for the nearest AED and to meet the ambulance. EVERY electric shock goes to hospital the same day, even if the person is up and talking and says they are fine: the heart can stop hours later. They do not drive themselves and they do not go back to work. Nothing is re-energised until a licensed electrical worker has found why it happened. Notify the office immediately. A shock treated by or under a doctor is a serious electrical incident (Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld) s 11) and the regulator must be notified immediately (Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 292) — that is a separate duty from notifying WHSQ under Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) s 38, and both apply." Also add "and an AED if the site has one" to the first line of the INJURY paragraph, because the kit is "in the van" and the plant room may be three levels down.

blocking.field: steps[2].hazards (electric shock from the crew's own equipment is absent) and steps[2].controls[1] and [2]
blocking.problem: steps[2].controls[1] instructs "have the wet vac in the room and plugged in — not in the van — before any water runs" and controls[2] instructs "Task light on the valve set". steps[5] then deliberately runs "Hundreds of litres of black stagnant riser water" across that same floor (steps[2].hazards[5] says "Hundreds to thousands of litres"), and steps[2].hazards[0] already concedes "Wet floor". The step's hazard list names slips, discharge reaching a switchroom, noise, poor lighting, lone working and unlawful disposal — but never electric shock from the 240 V leads, wet vac and task light the statement has just told the crew to put in the water. Nowhere in the file do the words RCD, safety switch, residual current device, extension lead or earth leakage appear. A worker in waterproof steel-cap boots standing in a conductive film of water on a concrete slab, with a damaged lead or a wet vac drawing water, is a fatality. The document's own reasoning makes this a legal breach as well as a design fault: whenRequired says "IS IT CONSTRUCTION WORK? Start from yes", and Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 140(2) requires that "all electrical equipment for the performance of construction work complies with the requirements of AS/NZS 3012 (Electrical installations—Construction and demolition sites)".
blocking.fix: Add to steps[2].hazards: "Electric shock from our own 240 V leads, task light and wet vac standing in the water this job puts on the floor". Insert a new control as steps[2].controls[0], ABOVE the existing engineering controls so it is read first, at level "engineering": "Every lead, the wet vac and the task light run through a portable RCD (safety switch) plugged in at the outlet, and you press its test button and see it trip before the drain opens. Leads are hung or run clear of the wet zone — never across the floor the water is going to reach, never through the bund. The task light is battery or extra-low voltage, not a 240 V worklight sitting at the valve set. No portable RCD on the van, no drain. Electrical equipment for construction work must comply with AS/NZS 3012 (Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 140)." Then amend the existing steps[2].controls[1] to read "...and have the wet vac in the room, on the RCD, and plugged in — not in the van — before any water runs." Add to siteSpecificPrompts: "Do you have a portable RCD on the van, and has it been tested today? Where will the leads run so they are not in the water?"

blocking.field: steps[8].controls[1] (level and position, relative to steps[8].controls[2])
blocking.problem: steps[8].controls[1] is "Fire pump and jockey pump controllers back to AUTO... and then stand there and watch the jockey cut in and cut out on its own pressure settings", and it sits at index 1. steps[8].controls[2] — "Walk the isolation list you wrote and point at every single point on it: booster, bypass, tank and pump, hydrant cross-connection, main stop valve. Every lock off, every tag off" — sits at index 2, below it. A crew reads down and does the first thing it can, so the pumps go back into AUTO while the tank suction, the bypass and the cross-connection may still be locked shut by the crew's own padlocks. That is precisely the hazard the document names at steps[3].hazards[0] ("running deadheaded against a shut or drained system... a diesel set that keeps running until somebody physically stops it") and repeats at steps[10].controls[1] ("A pump in auto against a shut valve will run deadheaded and destroy itself"). The document creates its own named hazard through its own control order. The mislabelling is what does it: returning a selector by hand and then confirming it by eye and by watching is administrative verification, not an engineering control, and the false level is what ranks it above the real one.
blocking.fix: Reorder steps[8].controls so the isolation-list walk comes before the pump restoration — move the current controls[2] up to index 1 — and re-level the pump control from "engineering" to "administrative". Then amend the pump control text to open with the precondition: "Only once every point on the isolation list is released and the pump suction — tank valve, town main, bypass — has been proved open, put the fire pump and jockey pump controllers back to AUTO. A controller returned to AUTO with a suction or discharge point still locked shut starts the pump against a shut valve. Confirm each selector by eye, photograph it against the arrival photo, then stand clear and watch the jockey cut in and cut out on its own pressure settings..." (rest unchanged).

blocking.field: steps[8].hazards, steps[8].controls (no PPE control) and steps[8].residualRisk
blocking.problem: steps[8] is the step where the gong is deliberately sounded ("Run the alarm test valve and prove the whole chain: water motor gong, pressure switch, FIP alarm", controls[3]) and where both pumps are returned to AUTO and run (controls[1]). Its six hazards are all administrative-failure hazards — valve part shut, pump left out of auto, lock left on, switch not proving, zone still isolated, pressures down. It names none of the physical hazards it creates: a fire pump starting without warning at the controller you are standing at, the rotating coupling and shaft, a hot exhaust and manifold on a diesel set, diesel exhaust accumulating in an enclosed pump room, and the noise of a water motor gong and a running fire pump at arm's length. The step carries no PPE control at all, while steps[2].controls[7] ("Hearing protection on before the gong runs") sits back in a step that has finished, and it claims a residual of "low". The words ventilation, exhaust, carbon monoxide, coupling and guard appear nowhere in the file.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[8].hazards: "Fire pump starting without warning at the controller you are standing at — rotating coupling and shaft, and a hot exhaust and manifold on a diesel set"; "Diesel exhaust accumulating in an enclosed pump room while the set runs"; "Water motor gong and a running pump at close range during the alarm test". Add an administrative control immediately before the pump restoration control: "Before either controller goes back to AUTO, call it out loud, stand clear of the pumpset and out of line with the coupling and the shaft, and keep everyone else out of the pump room. On a diesel set, check the pump room louvres and the exhaust are clear and the room is open to atmosphere before it runs, and nobody stays in the room longer than the test needs." Add a PPE control as the last entry in steps[8].controls: "Hearing protection on before the alarm test valve is opened and before either pump runs — the water motor gong and a running fire pump are both above the exposure standard at the distance you will be standing (Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 58 audiometric testing applies)." Change steps[8].residualRisk from "low" to "medium".

blocking.problem: steps[7] ("Refill, vent and re-pressurise") is rated initialRisk "high" and residualRisk "low". Two of its seven controls are engineering (fill through the bypass, vent at the high point); the controls standing between a worker and the two mechanisms that can kill in this step are purely procedural. Against "Re-pressurising while a cover is still off or someone is still on the riser" the only control is controls[2], "everyone's hands clear and CALLED clear — out loud, answered" — a spoken check. Against "Water hammer cracking a fitting or a gauge" the only control is controls[4], "Open the main stop valve a quarter turn at a time and watch the downstream gauge climb" — a judgement call. The document itself describes the energy involved at steps[5].hazards[0]: "a cover or flange letting go under 1000 kPa". steps[5], which handles that same stored pressure with better controls including two engineering ones and a stand-to-the-side rule, honestly rates medium. Refill is where an under-torqued cover actually lets go, and rating it low tells a crew the dangerous part is behind them.
blocking.fix: Change steps[7].residualRisk from "low" to "medium". If low is to be argued for, it needs an engineering control that removes the person rather than warns them — e.g. a control at level "engineering": "Bring the riser back up from outside the line of the alarm valve cover — nobody stands in front of the cover or the gauge glass while pressure is climbing, and the pressure is brought up on the bypass with the crew clear of the valve set until the downstream gauge holds steady."

blocking.problem: steps[1].hazards[3] is "Isolating at a point that also kills the hydrant supply", and steps[4].controls[0] then instructs the crew to actually shut it: "shut every supply on it — town main, tank and pump, alarm valve bypass, hydrant cross-connection and the fire brigade booster inlet." So the document contemplates leaving a building with dead hydrants. Nothing carries that anywhere. The only control offered against the hazard is steps[1].controls[4], "confirm the scope with the building manager in person" — which tells you to find out, not what to do about it. The impairment machinery is sprinkler-shaped throughout: steps[0].controls[3] lists interim measures as hot work stopped, a fire watch, extra extinguishers and tenants told, with no mention of hydrants; the permits list has no hydrant impairment; and the emergency FIRE paragraph tells the brigade only "whether the system is restored or could not be restored" — a brigade that arrives, is told the sprinklers are off, connects to a hydrant and gets nothing. That is how firefighters die.
blocking.fix: Append to steps[0].controls[1] (the written approval control): "If the isolation also takes out hydrants or a second building, that goes on the same impairment approval as its own line — which hydrants, which areas, start and finish time — and the monitoring centre and the building manager are told the hydrants are out as well as the sprinklers." Insert a new administrative control in steps[4], immediately after the booster-tag control: "Where the isolation takes the hydrant supply as well, tag the affected hydrant landing valves and the hydrant booster 'HYDRANTS IMPAIRED — NO WATER' with your name, mobile and the time it comes back, and tell the monitoring centre and the building manager separately. Hydrants out is its own impairment, not a footnote to the sprinkler one." In the emergency FIRE paragraph, after "tell the brigade the same thing the moment they arrive", add: "and tell them at the booster, BEFORE they connect, whether the hydrants are dead too and which ones." Add to siteSpecificPrompts: "Does this isolation take the hydrants as well, and who has been told?"

blocking.field: steps[6].controls[1] and steps[6].hazards; emergency (no EWP rescue)
blocking.problem: steps[6].controls[1] permits an EWP to be used under this statement ("work off a rated industrial platform ladder or an EWP with the Safe QLD heights statement attached"), hrcw[4] claims s 291(o) powered mobile plant for this statement, and ppe[8] and ppe[9] set out harness and restraint rules for a boom basket and a scissor lift — so the document part-owns EWP work rather than fully handing it over. Yet steps[6].hazards names cover weight, sharp edges, asbestos, dropped tools, awkward reach and falling more than 2m, and never names crush between the basket and the pipework, ductwork, cable tray or slab overhead — which in a plant room is the room's defining feature, and which is how most EWP operators are killed. The words crush, entrap, rescue, ground controls, emergency lowering and spotter appear nowhere in the file, and the emergency section — the part a crew reads on THIS statement while one of them is in a basket — has no response for an operator trapped against the structure or slumped at the controls. A harness in restraint, which is what ppe[8] correctly specifies, does nothing against sustained pressure crush; it is the wrong hazard.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[6].hazards: "Crush between the EWP basket and the pipework, ductwork, cable tray or slab overhead — sustained pressure trapping the operator against the controls". Insert a new administrative control immediately after steps[6].controls[1]: "In an EWP, look up before every movement and keep clearance to the pipework, ducts, cable tray and slab above the basket. Approach an overhead obstruction in the slowest boom range, never with the machine travelling, and never with your body between the rail and something overhead. A second person stays on the ground for the whole lift — shown the ground controls and the emergency lowering on that machine before it goes up, with the key and the machine's manual, and they do not leave the room." Add a paragraph to emergency: "EWP EMERGENCY. If the operator is trapped against the structure or slumped in the basket, the ground person brings the basket down on the ground controls or the emergency lowering valve — do not climb up to them. Ring 000 and say a worker is trapped in an elevating work platform at height. Nobody goes up in a basket in a plant room without a ground person who has been shown that machine's ground controls and emergency lowering." If instead the intent is that all EWP use leaves this statement, then steps[6].controls[1] must say so plainly ("no EWP is used under this statement") and hrcw s 291(o) and ppe[8]/[9] should be removed from it.
